WHAT IT MEANS
One contract instead of three

In a traditional remodel you hire an architect or designer, then take their drawings out to bid, then hire a builder. Three contracts, and when something doesn't work the designer blames the builder and the builder blames the drawings.

Design-build is one contract and one team: we design it, render it, price it, and build it. If something in the design won't build, we find out at the drawing stage, because it's our problem either way.

START TO FINISH
How a design-build project runs

Four phases, one contract. The same company draws it, prices it and builds it, so there is no handoff where the drawings stop being anyone’s responsibility.

THE DESIGN PHASE
What you get before anything is built

When a project changes the layout, design is its own phase with its own deliverables, under a design agreement that is credited toward construction. You keep what it produces whether or not we build the project.

✓

BATHROOM	from $2,500 for bathrooms

ADDITION OR WHOLE-HOME	from $10,000 for additions

Every design fee is credited in full toward your construction contract when you build with us. If you decide not to build, the drawings and renderings are yours and you owe nothing further.

WHEN IT DOESN’T APPLY
Not every project needs a design phase.

If your layout isn’t changing — same footprint, same plumbing, new finishes — we’ll measure, spec it and quote it. No design agreement, no fee. The design phase is for projects where the layout is genuinely in play, and we’ll tell you which one yours is on the first call.

DRAWINGS & CODE
When a licensed architect comes in

Not every project needs one. A kitchen that keeps its walls where they are is drawn, permitted and built without an architect involved. The moment a project moves structure — taking out a bearing wall, adding a second story, changing a roofline — the permit set has to be sealed by a licensed design professional, and that is where ours comes in. We prepare the drawings, a licensed New Jersey architect reviews, revises where needed, and seals them, and structural elements are engineered and stamped where the code requires it. You are not managing that relationship; it sits inside our contract. There is more detail on how this works on home additions, where it applies to almost every job.

PRICING
Priced against an approved design

A number produced before anyone has drawn the project is a guess, and guesses move. We price construction against drawings you have already approved, line by line, with allowances named for the things you have not chosen yet. That is why the design agreement comes first and why it is credited toward construction — the design is what makes a real price possible. Most of our kitchen projects run $60,000 to $140,000; if you want to see how the market breaks down before you talk to anyone, our kitchen remodel cost guide covers Bergen County ranges in detail.

WHO IT SUITS
Homeowners who want one accountable party

Design-build fits homeowners doing $60,000-and-up projects who would rather hold one company responsible for the drawings and the building than referee between two. It suits people who want to see the finished room before committing to it, and who would rather find a problem on a drawing than on a Tuesday with the walls open. It is a poor fit if you already have a completed, sealed set you are happy with and just want it priced — that is a plan review, not a design phase, and it is priced separately so you are not paying twice for the same work. You can see finished work in our Montclair kitchen case study.

COST & PLANNING GUIDE
What a Kitchen Remodel Really Costs in Bergen County (2026)
UPDATED JULY 2026 · BY HAMLETT RENOVATIONS

Most kitchen remodels in Bergen County run $25,000 to $70,000+. Where you land comes down to three things: the cabinets you choose, the countertops, and whether you're changing the layout. A cosmetic refresh with the walls staying put sits at the low end. A full gut — custom cabinets, stone counters, a wall coming down — sits at the top. Here's how to figure out which one is your kitchen, before anyone steps in your house.

Written by the team at Hamlett Renovations — a licensed, family-owned GC that's remodeled kitchens across Wayne, Franklin Lakes, Wyckoff, Ridgewood and the rest of Bergen, Passaic, Morris & Essex County since 2019.

That’s the market. Our own kitchens run $35,000 to $60,000 for a refresh that keeps the layout, and $60,000 to $140,000 for a full design-build — see kitchen design & build.

The short version: three price tiers
Tier	What you're getting	Typical cost
Refresh	Same layout. New cabinets (stock/semi-custom), counters, backsplash, fixtures, paint.	$25,000 – $40,000
Mid-range	Semi-custom or custom cabinets, stone counters, new lighting, maybe an island. Minor layout tweaks.	$40,000 – $60,000
Full custom / gut	Custom cabinetry, high-end stone, moved walls, new electrical/plumbing, premium appliances.	$60,000 – $70,000+

Two kitchens the same size can land in different tiers — it's the choices, not the square footage, that set the price.

What actually drives the cost
1. Cabinets — the single biggest line

Stock cabinets cost a fraction of custom, and on most Bergen County kitchens cabinetry is roughly a third of the whole budget. This is where you have the most control over the final number.

2. Countertops

Laminate to quartz to natural stone is a wide spread. Quartz is the North Jersey favorite right now — durable, and priced in the middle.

3. Layout changes

Keeping the sink, stove, and fridge where they are keeps costs down. The moment you move plumbing or take down a wall, you're adding labor, permits, and sometimes structural work.

4. Older homes

A lot of Bergen County housing stock is pre-1970. Open a wall in a 1940s colonial and you can find knob-and-tube wiring, undersized panels, or cast-iron plumbing that has to be brought up to code. It's what we plan for, and it's why the number accounts for what the house might turn up once it's open.

5. Permits

A kitchen remodel that touches electrical, plumbing, or walls needs a permit and inspections. We handle all permits and inspections on every job — you don't chase paperwork.

How long does a kitchen remodel take?

It depends on whether the layout changes. A refresh that leaves the walls, plumbing and appliance positions alone runs 3–6 weeks. A full design-build kitchen — moving walls, relocating plumbing and gas, upgrading electrical, new cabinetry — runs 10–14 weeks. The biggest schedule variable is usually cabinet lead time, so we order early and work around it.

What can blow a budget — and how to avoid it

The surprises are almost always behind the walls: old wiring, a rotted subfloor under the old dishwasher, or plumbing that isn't where the plans say. The fix isn't luck — it's a contractor who's opened enough Bergen County walls to price for what's likely there, and who tells you before the work starts, not after. Ask any contractor how they handle a mid-job surprise. The answer tells you a lot.

How to get a number you can actually trust

Online kitchen estimators guess. They don't know your wiring, your layout, or what's under your floor. The only accurate number comes from an on-site visit. We come out, look at the actual space, talk through what you want, and send back an itemized written quote — so you can see exactly what each part costs and where you can trade up or down. It's free, and there's no obligation. For the full breakdown of cabinetry tiers and countertops, see our kitchen remodeling services, or how design-build works end to end.

What's the cheapest way to remodel a kitchen?
+
Keep the layout, choose stock or semi-custom cabinets, and pick a durable mid-range counter like quartz. Not moving plumbing or walls is the single biggest saving.

What a Bathroom Remodel Really Costs in North Jersey (2026)
UPDATED JULY 2026 · BY HAMLETT RENOVATIONS

Most bathroom remodels in North Jersey run $12,000 to $35,000+. Where you land depends on the size of the room, the materials you pick, and how much gets moved — because the second you relocate a toilet or shower, you're into plumbing and labor that a same-layout remodel never touches. A guest bath refresh sits at the low end. A primary bath with custom tile, a walk-in shower, and a moved layout sits at the top.

Written by the team at Hamlett Renovations — a licensed, family-owned GC remodeling bathrooms across Wayne, Franklin Lakes, Wyckoff, Ridgewood and the rest of Bergen, Passaic, Morris & Essex County since 2019.

That’s the market. Our own bathrooms run $12,000 to $22,000 for a refresh that keeps the layout, and $22,000 to $40,000 for a full design-build — see bathroom design & build.

The short version: three price tiers
Tier	What you're getting	Typical cost
Guest / hall bath	Same layout. New tub or shower, tile, vanity, toilet, fixtures, lighting.	$12,000 – $18,000
Full remodel	Tub-to-walk-in-shower conversion, new tile floor + walls, vanity, better fixtures, minor layout tweaks.	$18,000 – $28,000
Primary / high-end	Custom tilework, double vanity, freestanding tub and walk-in shower, moved plumbing, heated floor.	$28,000 – $35,000+

A powder room and a primary suite are the same "project" on paper and wildly different numbers in reality — it's the room and the choices, not the label, that set the price.

What actually drives the cost
1. Size — and how much moves

A small hall bath with everything staying put is the cheapest remodel in the house. Move the toilet, tub, or vanity even a few feet and you're rerouting plumbing inside the floor and walls — the single biggest cost jump in any bathroom.

2. Tile

In a bathroom, tile is the biggest labor line. A simple subway wall is fast; intricate floor patterns, niches, and full-height shower tile take real hours. Material is cheap next to the labor to set it right.

3. Tub vs. walk-in shower

Converting a tub to a curbless walk-in shower is one of the most popular North Jersey requests right now — great for resale and aging-in-place, but it means new waterproofing, a re-sloped floor, and glass, so it adds cost over a like-for-like swap.

4. Waterproofing — the part you never see, and the part that matters most

Behind the tile, a proper moisture barrier and a correctly built shower pan are what keep water out of your walls and subfloor. Here's what most homeowners never think to ask: we don't lay a single tile until the waterproofing is done and tested. We confirm the pan and barrier hold water first — then the tile goes on. Skip that step, like a lot of quick jobs do, and a slow leak quietly rots your subfloor and grows mold behind the wall within a couple of years, where you can't see it until it's a big, expensive problem. Testing first is cheap insurance. Tearing out a two-year-old bathroom isn't.

5. Older homes

Open the wall in an older Bergen County bath and it's common to find cast-iron drains, a rotted subfloor under the old tub, or plumbing that has to be brought up to code. We plan and price for it instead of pretending it isn't there.

6. Permits

Anything touching plumbing or electrical needs a permit and inspection. We handle all permits and inspections on every job — you don't chase paperwork.

How long does a bathroom remodel take?

Most of our bathrooms run 2–4 weeks. A straight refresh is on the faster end; a full tile job (tile has to be set, then given time to cure before grouting) and any layout change push toward four. If it's your only bathroom, we'll talk through scheduling so you're never without one longer than necessary.

What can blow a budget — and how to avoid it

In bathrooms, the surprises are almost always water damage you couldn't see: rot under the old tub, a soft subfloor, or plumbing that's been quietly leaking behind the tile. The fix is a contractor who's opened enough old bathrooms to expect it, prices for it, and shows you before the work — not a change order sprung on you halfway through.

How to get a number you can actually trust

Online estimators can't see your plumbing, your subfloor, or what's behind your tile — so their numbers are guesses. The only accurate price comes from an on-site visit. We come out, look at the actual room, talk through what you want, and send back an itemized written quote so you can see exactly what each piece costs and where you can trade up or down. For the full breakdown, see our bathroom remodeling services, or how design-build works end to end.

Your backyard, made for spending time in

A good deck adds real living space — somewhere to grill, gather, and unwind a few steps from the kitchen door. We design yours to suit how your yard sits and how you'll use it, whether that's a simple platform or a multi-level space with railings, lighting, and built-in seating. Most of our outdoor projects do not stop at the deck: paver patios under and around it, retaining walls to hold a sloped yard, and pool surrounds are the same job and the same crew.

CHOOSING YOUR DECKING
Composite, pressure-treated, or hardwood?

The board you walk on drives both the look and the upkeep. Here's the honest trade-off between the three we build with most.

Composite
low upkeep

Capped composite boards (lines like Trex and TimberTech) resist fading, staining, and rot. More up front, but no sanding or sealing — an occasional wash and it's done.

Best for: homeowners who want the longest life and the least maintenance.
Pressure-treated
budget-friendly

The most affordable and widely available option. Strong and proven, but it needs periodic cleaning and sealing to keep its color and fight the weather.

Best for: tighter budgets and a classic wood look you don't mind maintaining.
Hardwood / cedar
natural beauty

Cedar, mahogany, and similar species bring warm, real-wood character and good natural durability. Periodic finishing keeps the tone rich.

Best for: a premium, natural look where the grain is the point.

When the space wasn’t built for what you’re doing

Most commercial fit-outs are a refresh. The space was an office and it stays an office — the systems already suit the use, and the work is layout and finishes.

The room used to be outside

At some point in this building’s life somebody enclosed a porch and called it living space. That happens constantly in older housing stock, and on the surface it works — you gain a room. What comes with it is a floor that was never built to be a floor.

A porch is deliberately pitched. It is sloped so rain runs off it, and that slope does not disappear when you put walls around it. Decades later it is still there, quietly out of level under whatever has been laid on top. You cannot shim your way out of that and you certainly cannot set cabinets and a countertop on it. The floor had to come out and be re-levelled in full before a single base cabinet went down.

The ceiling told the same story from the other direction: several different heights across one room, because the porch roof and the original house were never meant to meet.

And then the walls came off

Opening it up produced the rest of it, and none of it was visible on the day we quoted:

Mold behind the walls — which had to come out before anything went back
Exhaust fans venting into nothing. Fans that ran, made the right noise, and discharged straight into a cavity instead of outside
Electrical wire buried in the wall — concealed, with no way to get at it

Those first two belong together. A fan that vents into a wall cavity is not moving damp air out of the building; it is moving it somewhere it cannot escape from. Put that in an enclosed porch with a floor that never drained properly, and mold behind the plaster is not bad luck. It is arithmetic.

All of it was fixed before the kitchen went in — because the alternative is a beautiful room built on top of the same problem, which fails again in five years and takes the new kitchen with it.
